messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] 'Matt trick' for logistic-binomial model
parts:
A serious problem with your model is that you declare
sigma2 as having support (0,infinity)

real<lower=0> sigma2;

and then you use it with bounded support:

sigma2 ~ uniform(0,100);

What you need to do is declare sigma2 with support
that matches the model.

real<lower=0,upper=100> sigma2;

The re-encoding in model2 forgot the additive term for
the mean. Instead of

transformed parameters {
real u[G];
for (g in 1:G)
u[g] <- e_u[g] * sqrt(sigma2);
}

you need the assignment to include the mean u0:

for (g in 1:G)
u[g] <- u0 + e_u[g] * sqrt(sigma2);

but you really want to declare e_u as a vector:

vector[G] e_u;

and then vectorize the assignment:

u <- u0 + e_u * sqrt(sigma2);

In fact, for both speed and simplicity, I'd replace
prior for variance

sigma2 ~ uniform(0,100);

with a uniform prior on standard deviation (changing the
constraint on its support to upper=10, of course!):

sigma ~ uniform(0,10);

and then replace the vectorized assignment with

u <- u0 + e_u * sigma;

- Bob

parts:
Bob and Andrew,

Thanks for the helpful suggestions.  Right after I posted I realized that I had forgotten to incude the u0 term in the transformed parameters block.  I tried to pull the post once I realized my mistake.  After I put the mean term back in, things worked more or less as expected in terms of the estimates from the posterior.

If you don't mind, I have a couple of follow up questions...

1.  Andrew, is Bob's suggestion of using uniform(0,10) for sigma more in line with what you had in mind or were you thinking of something else?

2.  The effective sample size on all of the terms involved with transformed parameter block are surprisingly low.  I've attached the code (updated based on your suggestions) and results from a run using 4 chains with 10K iterations apiece.  Any thoughts on what is going on here?  While I'm definitely concerned about the effective sample size associated with sigma and u0, is there any need to worry about the e_u terms, or can we safely set these aside as a byproduct of the Matt trick. In short, do we expect viable sample sizes for things like the e_u terms?

3.  I ran into the Matt trick while looking into ways of speeding up the model.  One possibility is to run this in JAGS which has a dedicated glm module.  In discussing this point in another thread, Matt Hoffman alluded to the possibility of using the Matt trick in JAGS.  I decided to check this out, but started getting totally off-the-wall estimates for sigma.  As suggested by my original post, it is totally possible that I just goofed up the code (see attached).  If you have any thoughts, I'd love to hear them, though you should feel free to tell me to take a hike given that this is a Stan list and I can understand that you might not want to accidentally encourage possible defection, even if only in the very short term.  Even if you don't feel comfortable commenting on the JAGS code, is there any reason to believe that the Matt trick would be viable in one program but another?  I could imagine situations in which it didn't do much with respect to speed, but I have a tougher time seeing how it could actually produce nonsensical results.

Thanks again for all of your help.  All of these questions aside, Stan is a fine piece of software and I look forward to seeing where it goes.

Adam

I've attached a table which includes diagnostics from a series of models, two of which were run in Stan, one of which was run in JAGS, all called via R.  The first Stan model uses a conventional random intercept parameterization, while the second uses the Matt trick.  The JAGS model uses the conventional parameterization because, as mentioned before, the Matt trick code I wrote produces crazy estimates for sigma.  These estimates were pulled straight off the screen which means there may be a bit of an apples-and-oranges problem here when it comes to trying to compare effective sample size and R-hat between Stan and JAGS.  If you think this is a serious problem for the purposes of this discussion, I'm happy to go back and recalculate things.  Looking at these rough estimates, however, not only does JAGS seem to outpace Stan, but Stan without the Matt trick seems to better than Stan with the Matt trick.

Just to be clear about a couple of things...

1.  Times for Stan do not include the time taken to compile the models.
2.  I made sure to use set_cppo("fast"), though this type of thing wouldn't explain the divergence between alternative parameterizations in Stan.

What else could I be missing here?

Adam

Bob, Ben, and Andrew,

I redid the analysis used to produce the previous speed tests which, I forgot to mention, were only based on 2K iterations (hence why some of the R-hats were so high).  Here's what is going on in the setup of the new tests:

1.  I used 4 chains with 10K iterations.

2.  I estimated three additional models.  As per Bob's suggestion, the first uses the Matt trick as before, but initial values are set to zero.  The second uses the Matt trick, but the x variable has been mean centered via the use of a transformed data block.  The third model also uses a mean-centered x, but does not use the Matt trick.

3.  Output was produced using the monitor command so as to ensure comparability between Stan and JAGS, as per the discussion here.  This speaks to Bob's question regarding the calculation of effective sample size.  One thing I noticed is that the monitor results did not match the print results.  I might expect this when looking at the JAGS output, but this also happened in Stan as well.  My understanding is that the print output in Stan is based on the summary function.  How do the summary calculations differ from the monitor calculations?

Here's my reading of the findings:

1.  JAGS outpaces Stan by quite a bit, regardless of how the model is specified in Stan.

2.  Stan models which use the Matt trick seem to do worse than Stan models without the Matt trick.

3.  Models with and without the Matt trick differ in terms of which parameters they are able to efficiently estimate.  Models with the Matt trick do better with respect to bx as compared to u0 or sigma.  The opposite holds for models without the Matt trick.

4.  Mean centering doesn't seem to help much.

5.  To speak to Bob's earlier question, in terms of posterior variance Stan actually seems to be doing slightly better when we look at the standard deviation.  Things are obviously a bit different when we look at, say, the standard error of the mean which corrects for effective sample size. Overall, JAGS seems to be doing better here, in large part because of the fact that Stan does well with either u0 and sigma or bx, but not both.  More specifically, we see Stan without the Matt trick doing better than JAGS with to the standard error of the mean for u0 and sigma.  In contrast, if we either center x or set initial values to 0, we see Stan with the Matt trick doing better than JAGS with respect to the standard error of the mean for bx.

I have also attached the diagnostics requested by Bob and Ben.  These include both a traceplot for u0, sigma, and bx, as well as the pairs graph depicting chain-specific results (chains 1 and 2 are on the first page, while chains 3 and 4 are on the second).  To show the correlation between parameter estimates, I have also included a scatterplot matrix depicting draws for u0, sigma, bx, and five randomly chosen group effects (both transformed and untransformed). I'm not sure whether this is the best approach for answering Bob's question as to whether the traceplots show high correlation of the u0, sigma, and e_u variables.  In the first place, I'm not sure that what I did even counts as a traceplot in the usual sense. It would also be preferable to look at all of the u and e_u terms, but I couldn't think of a good way to do this given that I have 144 groups and, hence, 288 + 3 = 291 parameters to graph.  All graphs correspond to the row in the table labeled "Stan w/Matt" (i.e. I used the Matt trick but did not center x or force initial values to 0).

My read is that the chains for u0 and sigma aren't mixing especially well (at least not compared to bx) and that there is some correlation between sigma, u, and e_u, though maybe not a crazy amount.  The u terms seem okay, there is some evidence of correlation between sigma and the e_u terms, and there is definitely correlation among the e_u terms themselves.  Again, this approach is less than perfect because I'm only looking at a handful of u/e_u terms.  Things could be worse elsewhere in the model.

Adam

messages.subject: Cauchy vs. uniform priors for scales
parts:
Cauchy's just like any other prior. It's in the manual
section on regression and also documented in the distributions.
In Stan:

parameters {
real<lower=0> sigma;
...
model {
sigma ~ cauchy(0,5);
...

In JAGS, you just need to truncate, so it'd be this
if they have the cauchy

sigma ~ dcauchy(0,5) T[0,];

and otherwise you'll need to replace dcauchy with the
T distribution with 1 degree of freedom.

You need to truncate for the uniform in JAGS, too.

- Bob

TFM says for the chain_id argument to pairs():

By default, NULL, which will plot roughly half of the chains in the lower panel and the rest in the upper panel. Otherwise, an integer vector can be passed to select some subset of the chains, of which roughly half will be plotted in the lower panel and the rest in the upper panel. Or a list of two integer vectors, each specifying a subset of the chains to be plotted in the lower and upper panels respectively. The latter option can be useful if you suspect that one chain has failed to converge.

So, the i-j plot will never be identical to the j-i plot, unless you do something wasteful like chain_id = c(1,1). I'm not sure exactly what was passed for this plot, but if the i-j plot looks substantially different than the j-i plot, then it didn't converge.
